abstract: Using data from Upwork, a major online freelancing platform, this study examines how generative AI tools launched in 2022-2023 affected freelance workers. The authors find that freelancers in occupations more exposed to AI experienced a 2% decline in contracts and a 5% drop in earnings, with surprisingly negative effects concentrated among high-skill, experienced workers rather than less skilled workers. The findings suggest that generative AI compresses quality differences across skill levels, reducing clients' willingness to pay premiums for top-tier talent and necessitating policy reforms to protect vulnerable workers.
keyFindings: Freelancers in occupations more exposed to generative AI experienced a 2% decline in the number of monthly contracts and a 5% decrease in total monthly earnings following the 2022-2023 releases of ChatGPT, DALL-E2, and Midjourney.

High-skill and experienced freelancers with stronger past performance were disproportionately affected by AI, contradicting conventional wisdom that expertise insulates workers from technological disruption.

Generative AI appears to be 'leveling the playing field' by enabling lower-rated freelancers to produce outputs approximating top-tier quality, reducing clients' perceived value of paying premiums for high-reputation workers.
Negative employment and earnings effects persisted and grew over the six to eight months following AI model releases, suggesting permanent shifts in service valuation rather than temporary shocks.

The magnitudes of decline are comparable to impacts from major automation technologies like industrial robots and comparable to labor market effects of policy interventions like minimum wage changes and unionization access.
methodology: Empirical analysis using Upwork platform data, examining freelancer outcomes before and after the launch of generative AI models (image-based models DALL-E2 and Midjourney in early 2022, and text-based model ChatGPT in November 2022). The authors used these model launches as natural experiments, comparing changes in freelancer outcomes in AI-affected versus less-affected occupations in a difference-in-differences framework. Analysis identified occupations likely to be affected by different AI types (e.g., copyediting/proofreading for text-based AI; graphic design for image-based AI) and tracked employment and earnings outcomes over six to eight months post-launch. Data includes detailed information on contracts, earnings, client feedback, and platform-based reputational metrics.
qualifiers: Findings are limited to online freelance markets and may not fully capture dynamics of traditional employment arrangements or long-term contractual relationships. Analysis covers only the first six to eight months following AI model releases, which may not reflect longer-term labor market adjustments or the full scope of AI capability expansion. The study examines well-defined, task-oriented freelance jobs that are arguably more amenable to AI substitution than complex, collaborative work. Authors note that the future trajectory of AI remains difficult to predict as technology continues to evolve rapidly. Generalization to non-freelance workers and occupations beyond those studied should be considered tentative.
